note: Original practice questions for Science Olympiad Division B Botany, aligned to the 2027 topic list. Graph numbers are practice patterns for coaching, not data from a published study. The official rules take precedence.

topics.label: How people and animals use plants

questions.question: Which organelle captures light for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll inside the chloroplast absorbs light. Mitochondria release energy from food by cellular respiration. Plant cells have both.

questions.question: In a plant cell, the cell wall is outside the cell membrane.
questions.explanation: The cell membrane is the living boundary of the cell. The cellulose cell wall sits outside it and supports the cell.

questions.question: Select ALL structures that plant cells can have and typical animal cells do not.
questions.explanation: Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane. Plant cells also have a cellulose cell wall, and green cells have chloroplasts. A large central vacuole stores water and helps keep the cell firm.

questions.question: Name each labeled part of the root tip.
questions.explanation: The root cap protects the tip as it pushes through soil. The apical meristem divides. Cells lengthen in the zone of elongation. Root hairs, farther up, add surface area for water and minerals.

questions.question: Root hairs help a plant mostly by
options: adding surface area for taking in water and minerals
questions.answer: adding surface area for taking in water and minerals
questions.explanation: Each root hair is a long extension of an epidermal cell. More surface area means more contact with water and minerals in the soil.

questions.question: Name the waterproof strip in the endodermis that forces water to cross a cell membrane before it enters the vascular tissue.
questions.explanation: The Casparian strip is a waxy band in the cell walls of the endodermis. Water cannot sneak between those cells, so it must pass through a living cell. The plant can then control which minerals enter the xylem.

questions.question: How are vascular bundles usually arranged in a monocot stem?
options: In one ring near the outside
questions.explanation: Corn is a clear example: its bundles are scattered. A dicot stem, such as a bean, usually has bundles in a ring. That ring is one reason many dicots can add wood.

questions.question: In a young dicot stem, xylem is usually toward the inside of each vascular bundle and phloem toward the outside.
questions.explanation: In a typical young dicot bundle, xylem faces the center of the stem and phloem faces the outside. Remember: xylem carries water, phloem carries sugars.

questions.question: What meristem makes a stem or root grow longer?
questions.explanation: Apical meristems sit at shoot tips and root tips. Their cell divisions cause primary growth, which adds length. The vascular cambium causes thickening, not length.

questions.question: Name each labeled part of the leaf cross section.
questions.explanation: The waxy cuticle limits water loss. Palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts and do much of the photosynthesis. Spongy mesophyll has air spaces for gases. A stoma is a pore between guard cells. The vein holds xylem and phloem.

questions.question: What is the main job of stomata?
options: Carry water up from the roots inside xylem
Let gases in and out of the leaf
questions.answer: Let gases in and out of the leaf
questions.explanation: Stomata are pores, often on the underside of a leaf. Carbon dioxide enters, and oxygen and water vapor leave. Guard cells open and close each pore.

questions.stimulus: The line shows a typical daily pattern of transpiration for a watered plant on a sunny day. The numbers are relative units for practice, not a published data set.
questions.question: At which time is transpiration highest?
questions.explanation: On a typical sunny day the rate is low at dawn and at night, when stomata are mostly closed, and highest around midday. Clouds, dry air, and dry soil can change a real plant's curve.

questions.question: Ferns spread using spores. Where are those spores made on many ferns?
questions.explanation: A sorus is a cluster of sporangia, often a brown dot on the underside of a fern frond. Each sporangium releases spores. Ferns do not make seeds or fruits.

questions.question: Mosses make seeds inside cones.
questions.explanation: Mosses reproduce with spores. They do not make seeds or cones. Cones are a gymnosperm structure, as in pines.

questions.question: Select ALL that usually disperse by spores rather than seeds.
questions.explanation: Mosses and ferns are seedless. A pine makes seeds in cones, and a sunflower makes seeds inside a fruit. A seed contains a multicellular embryo. A spore is usually a single reproductive cell.

questions.question: Name each labeled part of the flower. The thin stalk under the yellow anther is drawn, but it is not one of the letters.
questions.explanation: Petals often attract pollinators. Sepals cover the bud. The anther makes pollen and sits on a filament; together they are the stamen. The stigma is the sticky top of the pistil. The ovary holds ovules, which can become seeds. The ovary can become the fruit.

questions.question: Name each labeled part of this opened bean seed.
questions.explanation: The seed coat protects the seed. A bean has two cotyledons, which store food. The radicle is the embryonic root and the plumule is the embryonic shoot. Together with the rest of the tiny plant, they are the embryo.

questions.question: Which part is the male, pollen-making structure of a flower?
questions.explanation: A stamen is an anther plus its filament. The anther produces pollen. The pistil (stigma, style, and ovary) is the female structure.

questions.question: From the top of the pistil down to the bottom, the parts are
questions.explanation: Pollen lands on the stigma. The pollen tube grows down the style. Fertilization happens in an ovule inside the ovary.

questions.question: Select ALL that are fruits in botany. A fruit develops from a flower and holds seeds.
questions.explanation: A tomato is a berry, and a bean pod is the ovary wall around the seeds. An apple is a fruit too, even though some of the flesh grows from tissue outside the ovary. A potato is a stem tuber, not a fruit.

questions.question: What does secondary growth do to a woody stem?
options: Makes it longer from the tip only
questions.explanation: Secondary growth adds tissue from the vascular cambium, including wood (secondary xylem). Length comes from primary growth at the apical meristems.

questions.question: Differentiation is when cells become specialized for particular jobs.
questions.explanation: Growth makes more cells or larger cells. Differentiation is the next idea: a cell may become a xylem cell, a guard cell, or a root-hair cell, each with its own job.

questions.question: Which tissue carries sugars from leaves to the rest of the plant?
questions.explanation: Phloem moves sugars, often as sucrose, from sources such as leaves to sinks such as roots, fruits, and growing tips. Xylem moves water and minerals upward.

questions.question: What is the loss of water vapor from a plant called?
questions.explanation: Most transpiration happens through open stomata. It pulls water up the xylem and also cools the leaf. Some water is lost through the cuticle, but much less.

questions.question: Root pressure is the main reason water can reach the top of a tall tree.
questions.explanation: Root pressure can push water a short distance. In a tall tree, water is pulled up the xylem as transpiration evaporates water from the leaves. Water molecules stick to each other (cohesion) and to the xylem wall (adhesion). This is the cohesion-tension theory.

questions.question: Which plant is a monocot?
questions.explanation: Corn has one cotyledon, parallel leaf veins, and flower parts in multiples of three. Beans, oaks, and sunflowers are dicots (eudicots).

questions.question: Select ALL typical features of a dicot (eudicot).
options: Leaf veins that usually form a net
Flower parts often in fours or fives
Vascular bundles scattered through the stem
answer: Leaf veins that usually form a net
Flower parts often in fours or fives
questions.explanation: Scattered stem bundles are typical of monocots. Dicots usually have two cotyledons, netlike veins, flower parts in fours or fives, and stem bundles in a ring. Many biologists now use the name eudicot for this group.

questions.question: Kelp is a large alga. It does not have true roots, stems, and leaves.
questions.explanation: Kelp can be many meters long, so algae are not all single-celled. It has a holdfast, a stipe, and blades. Those parts do similar jobs to roots, stems, and leaves, but they are not the true organs of a land plant.

questions.question: Which organism is a cryptogam?
questions.explanation: Cryptogam is an older word for a plant that reproduces with spores instead of seeds, such as a moss or fern. A fern is also an embryophyte, meaning a land plant. Pines and flowering plants make seeds, so they are not cryptogams.

questions.question: Which organism is an embryophyte?
questions.explanation: Embryophytes are land plants. The embryo develops inside the parent. Mosses, ferns, and flowering plants are embryophytes. Kelp, diatoms, and Spirogyra are algae.

questions.question: A tree that adds a new ring of wood each year is best described as
questions.explanation: Woody plants keep aboveground stems and add secondary xylem, which is wood. Herbaceous plants do not build a persistent woody stem. Annual rings can show a year of that thickening.

questions.question: Who is often called the Father of Botany for early written studies of plants?
questions.explanation: Theophrastus, a student of Aristotle, wrote early books describing plants and how they grow. Later scientists built on that start.

questions.question: Who developed the two-word system of scientific names used for plants?
questions.explanation: Carl Linnaeus (also written Carolus Linnaeus) made binomial nomenclature the standard: a genus name plus a species epithet, as in Zea mays.

questions.question: Who used the word cells for the little rooms he saw in cork?
questions.explanation: In 1665 Hooke looked at thin slices of cork with a microscope and called the empty boxes cells. Those boxes were the walls of dead plant cells.

questions.question: Gregor Mendel discovered patterns of inheritance by studying
questions.explanation: Mendel tracked traits such as seed shape and plant height in garden peas. His counts led to the ideas of dominant and recessive factors, which we now call alleles.

questions.question: A heterozygous plant has two different alleles for a gene.
questions.explanation: Hetero means different. A plant with alleles T and t is heterozygous. A plant with TT or tt is homozygous.

questions.stimulus: Practice counts: a class grew offspring from two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt × Tt). T (tall) is dominant to t (short).
questions.question: About what fraction of the offspring were short?

table.caption: Practice counts from a Tt × Tt cross

questions.explanation: 24 short plants out of 97 is close to 1/4. A Punnett square for Tt × Tt predicts 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so about 3 tall : 1 short. Real counts rarely match the ratio exactly.

questions.question: In mosses, the green mat you usually notice is the
questions.explanation: Plants alternate generations. In mosses the familiar green plant is the gametophyte, the stage that makes gametes. A sporophyte grows out of it and makes spores. In ferns and flowering plants, the plant you notice is the sporophyte.

questions.question: Which pair is produced by photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: A simple form of the reaction is carbon dioxide + water + light energy → glucose + oxygen. Chlorophyll in the chloroplast captures the light.

questions.stimulus: The bars show a typical absorption pattern for chlorophyll a. The heights are relative practice values, not one lab's measurements.
questions.question: Which color of light is absorbed the least?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll a absorbs blue and red light strongly and absorbs green light poorly. Leaves look green because much of the green light is reflected.

questions.question: Plant cells carry out cellular respiration only at night.
questions.explanation: Plants break down glucose for energy both day and night. Photosynthesis needs light, so it stops in the dark. Respiration does not.

questions.question: In the scientific name Zea mays (corn), Zea is the
questions.explanation: A scientific name is a genus plus a species epithet. Zea is the genus. mays is the species epithet. The family of grasses is Poaceae.

questions.question: In a scientific name, the second word (the species epithet) is capitalized.
questions.explanation: The genus is capitalized and the species epithet is lowercase. The whole name is italicized or underlined, as in Zea mays.

questions.question: A waxy cuticle helps a land plant mainly by
options: absorbing soil minerals through the leaf
questions.explanation: Life on land dries a plant out. A waxy cuticle covers the epidermis and slows evaporation. Stomata then let the plant exchange gases without leaving the whole surface open.

questions.question: In the fossil record, flowering plants appear before ferns.
questions.explanation: Early land plants and ferns appear long before flowers. Seed plants such as gymnosperms also appear before flowering plants. Angiosperms, the flowering plants, become common much later.

questions.question: Bacteria in the root nodules of beans and other legumes help the plant mainly by
options: fixing nitrogen from the air into a form the plant can use
questions.answer: fixing nitrogen from the air into a form the plant can use
questions.explanation: Rhizobium and its relatives live in the nodules and fix nitrogen. The plant shares sugars. This mutualism is an important step in the nitrogen cycle.

questions.question: Select ALL that a plant must take in for photosynthesis.
options: Oxygen used as a raw material to build glucose
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water, using light energy. Oxygen is released as a product. It is not a raw material that gets built into the sugar.

questions.question: Cotton thread is made from
questions.explanation: Cotton fibers are long hairs that grow on the seed coat. People spin those hairs into thread. The fibers are almost pure cellulose.

questions.question: Select ALL materials that come from plants.
questions.explanation: Cotton and flax are plant fibers. Natural rubber is latex, often from the rubber tree. Wool is hair from sheep, so it is not a plant material.

questions.question: Allelopathy is when a plant
options: releases chemicals that help or harm nearby plants
questions.answer: releases chemicals that help or harm nearby plants
questions.explanation: Black walnut is a famous example. Its roots and husks release juglone, which keeps some neighboring plants from growing well. That is one way plants compete besides grabbing light, water, and minerals.

questions.stimulus: Practice data: average height of two plants grown alone and grown in the same pot. These numbers were made for practice.
questions.question: Which claim fits the graph?
options: Plant B lost more height than Plant A
Plant A lost more height when the plants grew together than Plant B did
Both plants grew taller together than they did alone
The two treatments gave each plant the same height
questions.answer: Plant A lost more height when the plants grew together than Plant B did
questions.explanation: Plant A drops from 40 cm alone to 22 cm together, a loss of 18 cm. Plant B drops from 30 cm to 28 cm, a loss of 2 cm. Growing together hurt Plant A more. That pattern fits competition, though this particular graph is practice data.

questions.question: A genetically modified plant is a plant that
options: has had its DNA changed by genetic engineering
is any plant a farmer chooses to grow
questions.answer: has had its DNA changed by genetic engineering
questions.explanation: Genetic engineering adds, removes, or edits DNA directly. Watering, transplanting, or simply choosing a plant to grow does not make it a GMO.

questions.question: Saving seeds from the best plants is the same method as making a genetically modified organism.
questions.explanation: Saving seeds from favored plants is traditional breeding. It changes crops over many generations, but it does not directly edit DNA the way genetic engineering does. Both can be used in farming. They are different methods.

questions.question: Which food is a root?
questions.explanation: A carrot is a taproot. A potato is a stem tuber. Broccoli is a cluster of flower buds. A celery stalk is a petiole, the stalk of a leaf.

questions.question: Select ALL of these foods that are roots.
questions.explanation: Carrots, beets, and radishes are storage roots. A potato is an underground stem. You can tell a potato is a stem because it has buds, the eyes.

questions.question: A shortage of nitrogen usually yellows which leaves first?
options: Brand-new leaves, while older leaves stay dark green
questions.explanation: Nitrogen can move out of older leaves to feed new growth, so older leaves yellow first. Iron does not move as easily, so an iron shortage yellows young leaves first, often between the veins.

questions.question: Select ALL that can make a plant look sick or grow poorly.
options: Too little nitrogen in the soil
Plenty of chlorophyll in a healthy leaf
answer: Too little nitrogen in the soil
questions.explanation: Fungi, viruses, and bacteria can infect plants. A missing nutrient, such as nitrogen, can also cause poor growth and yellow leaves. Plenty of chlorophyll is a sign of a healthy leaf, not a cause of sickness.

questions.question: If a leaf is yellow, the cause must be a virus.
questions.explanation: Yellowing, called chlorosis, can come from too little nitrogen or iron, from waterlogged soil, or from infection. Color alone does not tell you the cause.

questions.question: A flower has stamens and a pistil, but it has no petals. It is
questions.explanation: Complete means all four sets of parts: sepals, petals, stamens, and pistil. Perfect means both stamens and a pistil are present. Missing petals makes this flower incomplete, and it is still perfect.

questions.question: Name the lateral meristem that adds wood (secondary xylem) and secondary phloem.
questions.explanation: The vascular cambium is a thin layer of dividing cells between wood and bark. Cells it makes toward the inside become secondary xylem (wood). Cells toward the outside become secondary phloem.

questions.question: Wood is mostly
questions.explanation: Each year's secondary xylem builds the wood of a trunk. Secondary phloem is part of the inner bark and does not pile up the same way. The epidermis is only the young outer layer.

questions.question: Which idea best explains how a continuous column of water is pulled to the top of a tall tree?
options: Phloem pumping sugars up the trunk
questions.explanation: Transpiration at the leaves pulls on the water column. Cohesion keeps water molecules stuck to one another, and adhesion helps them stick to the xylem wall. Root pressure is real but too weak to supply the top of a tall tree. Stomata let water vapor out. They are not where water enters.

questions.question: The familiar leafy fern plant is the
questions.explanation: The large fern makes spores, so it is the sporophyte. Its gametophyte is a small, often heart-shaped plant that makes eggs and sperm. In mosses it is the other way around: the green mat is the gametophyte.

questions.question: In a chloroplast, the Calvin cycle (the sugar-building reactions) happens in the
questions.explanation: The stroma is the fluid inside the chloroplast. The Calvin cycle uses carbon dioxide there to build sugar. The light-catching reactions happen in the thylakoid membranes.

questions.question: Iron does not move easily inside a plant. An iron shortage usually shows first as
options: yellowing of the oldest leaves only
yellowing between the veins of young leaves
a powdery fungus on the stem
questions.answer: yellowing between the veins of young leaves
questions.explanation: Iron stays in older leaves, so new leaves run short first. The tissue between veins turns yellow while veins may stay green. Nitrogen is mobile, so a nitrogen shortage yellows older leaves first. A powdery coating suggests a fungus, not an iron shortage.

questions.question: In the fossil record, seeds appear before flowers.
questions.explanation: Seed plants such as early gymnosperms appear before flowering plants. Flowers and fruits are the later angiosperm traits. Ferns and other spore plants are older still.

questions.question: Which path returns carbon dioxide to the air from sugars a plant made?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis stores carbon in sugars. Cellular respiration in plants, animals, and decomposers releases carbon dioxide again. Transpiration moves water, and nitrogen fixation moves nitrogen, not this carbon.

questions.question: In this plant cell, the large pale-blue oval is the
questions.imageAlt: Plant cell with a thick wall, a round nucleus, small green chloroplasts, and a large pale-blue oval.
questions.explanation: The central vacuole is the big water-filled sac. The round green body with a dark center is the nucleus. The small green ovals are chloroplasts. The thick border is the cell wall.

questions.question: Select ALL structures you can see in this drawing.
questions.imageAlt: Plant cell with a thick wall, a round nucleus, small green chloroplasts, and a large pale-blue oval.
questions.explanation: The thick border is the cell wall, the small green ovals are chloroplasts, and the large pale oval is the central vacuole. Centrioles are an animal-cell structure and are not drawn here.

questions.question: Which drawing shows a fibrous root system?
questions.imageAlt: Two root systems under a soil-surface line. The left has one thick root with side branches. The right has many similar roots.
options: The left drawing, with one thick main root
The right drawing, with many similar roots
questions.answer: The right drawing, with many similar roots
questions.explanation: A fibrous system is a cluster of roots of similar size, common in grasses. The left drawing is a taproot: one main root with smaller branches.

questions.question: The left-hand root system, with one thick main root, is the kind a carrot or dandelion uses to store food.
questions.imageAlt: Two root systems under a soil-surface line. The left has one thick root with side branches. The right has many similar roots.
questions.explanation: That left drawing is a taproot. Carrots and dandelions store food in a thick main root. Grasses use the fibrous system on the right.

questions.question: Which stem cross section is typical of a monocot such as corn?
questions.imageAlt: Two stem cross sections. The left has vascular bundles in a ring. The right has bundles scattered through the stem.
options: The left circle, with bundles in a ring
The right circle, with bundles scattered through the stem
questions.answer: The right circle, with bundles scattered through the stem
questions.explanation: Monocot stems usually have vascular bundles scattered in the ground tissue. Many dicot stems have the bundles in a ring, like the left circle.

questions.question: The left-hand circle has vascular bundles arranged in a ring. That pattern is typical of which major flowering-plant group?
questions.imageAlt: Two stem cross sections. The left has vascular bundles in a ring. The right has bundles scattered through the stem.
questions.explanation: A ring of bundles is the usual dicot (eudicot) stem pattern. The scattered pattern on the right is typical of monocots.

questions.question: The tall, tightly packed cells just under the upper surface are
questions.imageAlt: Leaf cross section with a top layer, a row of tall dark cells, a layer of round cells, and a small pore on the lower surface.
questions.explanation: Palisade cells stand in columns under the upper epidermis and hold many chloroplasts. The rounder cells below them are spongy mesophyll, with air spaces. The small opening on the lower surface is a stoma.

questions.question: Name the small opening in the lower surface of this leaf.
questions.imageAlt: Leaf cross section with a top layer, a row of tall dark cells, a layer of round cells, and a small pore on the lower surface.
questions.explanation: A stoma is a pore between guard cells. Open stomata let carbon dioxide in and water vapor out.

questions.question: The orange clusters on these leaflets are
questions.imageAlt: A fern frond with green leaflets and many small orange clusters.
questions.explanation: A sorus (plural sori) is a cluster of sporangia, usually on the underside of a fern leaflet. Spores form there. Ferns do not make seeds.

questions.question: The plant in this drawing reproduces with seeds enclosed in fruit.
questions.imageAlt: A fern frond with green leaflets and many small orange clusters.
questions.explanation: The orange clusters are sori, where ferns make spores. Seeds enclosed in fruit are an angiosperm feature.

questions.question: The large orange parts of this flower are the
questions.imageAlt: A flower with orange petals, green sepals, pale stamens, and a green pistil in the center.
questions.explanation: Petals are often the showy parts that attract pollinators. The smaller green parts at the base are sepals. The center holds the stamens and the pistil.

questions.question: The green structure in the very center, with a dark tip, is the female part of the flower. What is it called?
questions.imageAlt: A flower with orange petals, green sepals, pale stamens, and a green pistil in the center.
questions.explanation: The pistil (made of one or more carpels) has a stigma at the tip, a style, and an ovary. The pale structures around it are stamens, which make pollen.

questions.question: The orange region at the tip, opposite the growth arrow, is the
questions.imageAlt: A root tip colored in bands, with an orange tip and an arrow marked growth direction.
questions.explanation: The root cap covers the tip and protects the dividing cells as the root pushes through soil. Growth continues back from that tip, in the direction of the arrow.

questions.question: The darkest green band just above the orange tip is where most new root cells are produced. That band is the
questions.imageAlt: A root tip colored in bands, with an orange tip and an arrow marked growth direction.
questions.explanation: The apical meristem, in the zone of cell division, sits just behind the root cap. Cells lengthen in the zone of elongation. Root hairs appear farther up, in the zone of maturation.

questions.question: In this diagram, water moves from the roots up to the leaves in the
questions.imageAlt: A plant column with leaves at the top and roots at the bottom. A blue pipeline is labeled xylem, water up. An orange pipeline is labeled phloem, sugar down.
questions.explanation: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals upward. Phloem carries sugar from the leaves toward the rest of the plant, including the roots.

questions.question: The main pull that draws water up the blue pipeline is
questions.imageAlt: A plant column with leaves at the top and roots at the bottom. A blue pipeline is labeled xylem, water up. An orange pipeline is labeled phloem, sugar down.
options: the root cap pushing soil aside
questions.explanation: Water evaporates from leaves through stomata. That transpiration pull, plus water molecules sticking together, draws the water column up the xylem.

questions.question: Which drawing lets carbon dioxide into the leaf?
questions.imageAlt: Two pairs of guard cells. The left pair is closed. The right pair is open, with carbon dioxide going in and oxygen plus water going out.
questions.explanation: When guard cells bend apart, the pore opens. Carbon dioxide can enter for photosynthesis, and water vapor can leave.

questions.question: A plant is most likely to use the closed pair when it needs to
questions.imageAlt: Two pairs of guard cells. The left pair is closed. The right pair is open, with carbon dioxide going in and oxygen plus water going out.
questions.explanation: Closing stomata cuts the path for water vapor. The tradeoff is that less carbon dioxide can enter, so photosynthesis slows.

questions.question: Select ALL substances this diagram shows leaving the chloroplast.
questions.imageAlt: A chloroplast with light, carbon dioxide, and water going in, and oxygen and sugar coming out.
questions.explanation: Light, carbon dioxide, and water go in. Photosynthesis stores energy in sugar and releases oxygen.

questions.question: Which group on this line encloses its seeds in a fruit?
questions.imageAlt: Four groups in a row: bryophyte, fern, gymnosperm, and angiosperm, with a note that seed and water independence increase toward the right.
questions.explanation: Angiosperms are the flowering plants. Their seeds develop inside a fruit. Gymnosperms have seeds, but the seeds are not enclosed in a fruit. Bryophytes and ferns use spores.

questions.question: Select ALL groups on this line whose sperm must swim through water to reach the egg.
questions.imageAlt: Four groups in a row: bryophyte, fern, gymnosperm, and angiosperm, with a note that seed and water independence increase toward the right.
questions.explanation: Mosses and ferns still need a film of water for fertilization. Gymnosperms and angiosperms deliver sperm through a pollen tube, so they are less tied to wet conditions.

questions.question: On this cycle, the stage that grows right after gametes fuse is the
questions.imageAlt: A life-cycle circle: sporophyte, spores made by meiosis, gametophyte, and gametes fusing.
questions.explanation: Fertilization joins two gametes and starts the diploid sporophyte. That sporophyte later makes haploid spores by meiosis.

questions.question: The gametophyte is already haploid. It produces gametes by
questions.imageAlt: A life-cycle circle: sporophyte, spores made by meiosis, gametophyte, and gametes fusing.
questions.explanation: Meiosis happens when the sporophyte makes spores, which is why the spores are marked n. The haploid gametophyte then makes gametes by mitosis, so the chromosome number does not get cut in half again.

questions.question: Photosynthesis moves carbon into plants from which part of this diagram?
questions.imageAlt: A cycle linking atmosphere, plants, consumers and decomposers, and soil nutrients.
options: The plant's roots, with no carbon in the air
questions.explanation: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and build sugars. Animals and decomposers return carbon to the air and nutrients to the soil.

questions.question: Which circle in this diagram includes the organisms that break dead plants down and return nutrients to the soil?
questions.imageAlt: A cycle linking atmosphere, plants, consumers and decomposers, and soil nutrients.
questions.explanation: Decomposers, grouped here with consumers, release nutrients from dead material back into the soil. Plants then take those nutrients up again.

questions.question: In this sequence, the stage immediately after pioneer grasses is
questions.imageAlt: A timeline from bare ground to pioneer grasses, then shrubs, then a climax forest.
questions.explanation: This is ecological succession. Bare ground is colonized by pioneer grasses, then shrubs, and later a taller climax forest.

questions.question: On this diagram, the climax forest is the earliest stage.
questions.imageAlt: A timeline from bare ground to pioneer grasses, then shrubs, then a climax forest.
questions.explanation: Time runs from bare ground toward the climax forest. The climax community is the later, more stable stage, not the first one.

questions.question: Older leaves are yellow while the newest growth stays green. That pattern is typical of a shortage of
questions.imageAlt: A plant with yellow older leaves and green new growth at the bottom of the stem.
options: water only, with no mineral involved
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is mobile. A short plant moves it out of older leaves and into new growth, so the older leaves yellow first. The drawing is a deficiency symptom, not an infectious disease.

questions.question: Both curves dip lowest in the middle of the graph. Leaves look green mainly because chlorophyll absorbs the least light in which region?
questions.imageAlt: Graph of absorbance versus wavelength for chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b, with a visible-light color bar.
questions.credit: Graph: Wikimedia Commons, File:Chlorophyll_ab_spectra-en.svg, CC BY-SA 3.0.
options: Green, near the middle of the color bar
questions.answer: Green, near the middle of the color bar
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b absorb strongly in the blue-violet and red, and weakly in the green. Green light is reflected or passed through, so leaves look green.

questions.question: On the right side of the graph, which pigment reaches a high peak at the longer wavelength?
questions.imageAlt: Graph of absorbance versus wavelength for chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b, with a visible-light color bar.
questions.credit: Graph: Wikimedia Commons, File:Chlorophyll_ab_spectra-en.svg, CC BY-SA 3.0.
options: Both peak at the same wavelength
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll a’s red peak sits farther right, near the long-wavelength end of red. Chlorophyll b’s red peak is a bit farther left. Both still absorb red light; they do not absorb it at exactly the same wavelength.
